A motorcycle is an awkward guest in southern Greenland, and Igaliku is the reason to think about it carefully. There is no road network linking the settlements here; you reach them by boat, helicopter, or on foot, and the tracks between the farms are short and local. Nevertheless this is one of the great historical landscapes of the Arctic, and it deserves a place in any ride that dreams about the edge of the map.

Around the year 1000 Norse settlers led by Erik the Red arrived in the fjords of southern Greenland, and they stayed for about four centuries. Igaliku, then called Garðar, became the seat of the bishop of Greenland in the twelfth century, with a stone cathedral and a large farm, and the remains of the cathedral and great barns can still be seen beside the modern village. Nobody knows precisely why the Norse colony disappeared, whether climate, trade, conflict or a mixture, and the silence of the ruins only makes the question louder. UNESCO lists the area under the name Kujataa, recognising both the Norse farms and the Inuit hunting culture that later took over.

The village today is small and quiet, with a handful of houses, a guesthouse, a tiny church and sheep grazing on the green slopes. Farming is possible here because of the sheltered fjord climate, and you can see hayfields, vegetable plots and even potatoes growing in the thin soil. The scenery is unlike anywhere else: grass-covered hills rolling down to the water, icebergs drifting in the fjord, and mountains with snow on their tops even in summer. The light is long and clear in June and July, and the air is cold, clean and still.

Narsaq, nearly forty kilometres away, is the nearest town and has the shops and fuel for the district, but do not expect to ride the distance on a road. Plan your travel with local boat operators or helicopter services, check conditions, and bring warm, waterproof clothing even in July. The best time is June to August, when the sea is open and the days are long. If you reach Igaliku, walk slowly, respect the ruins and the grazing animals, and leave only footprints.

Greenland has no roads between its towns, and in the south, where the green fjords of Kujataa lie, that fact is both a limit and a charm. The Norse came here in the late tenth century, led by Erik the Red, who settled at Brattahlíð, now the farm of Qassiarsuk, and for nearly five hundred years there were farms, churches and a bishop at Garðar, today's Igaliku. The settlers raised cattle, sheep and goats and hunted seals and walrus, and then, around the fifteenth century, they vanished, for reasons still debated, among them climate, trade and conflict. The Inuit farmers and hunters who live there now raise sheep on the same pastures, and UNESCO listed the Kujataa landscape in 2017 as an example of farming at the edge.

Sissarluttoq is a place name in this district, near Narsaq and Qaqortoq, and I cannot describe a specific site with certainty. What I can say is that the fjord country is green in summer, with grassy slopes, icebergs drifting down from the ice cap, and farms with hay bales wrapped in plastic. The light is clean and long, with a midsummer sun that barely sets, and the water is a deep, cold blue.

The only way here is by air to Narsarsuaq or by boat along the coast. There are short gravel roads between farms and villages, but no network to ride on, so a motorbike is a thing for another trip. Narsaq has about sixteen hundred people and Qaqortoq about three thousand, the biggest town in the south, with shops, a harbour, a museum and the open-air sculpture of the Stone and Man project, carved into the rocks of the town. Fuel is for boats and a few vehicles, and nobody is going to sell petrol to a visitor casually.

Summer, from June to August, is the season, with warm days, mosquitoes and the odd iceberg tsunami. Walking is the way to move, by trail or boat, past ruined Norse walls to the church of Hvalsey, a ruin standing by the water. Pack a thick jacket, a head net and patience, and plan for the weather to change the plan.

The last time anyone wrote about a living person at Hvalsey, they were writing about a wedding. In September 1408, a couple were married in the church there, and that is the final entry in the written record of the Norse settlement in Greenland. What happened afterwards, whether people died out, left or moved on, is still a mystery. The ruin, which the Greenlanders call Qaqortukulooq, is the best-preserved Norse building in the country, a church of grey stone with high gables, built around the year 1300, standing beside a small bay under green hills, with its walls still more than four metres high.

Erik the Red settled this region in about 985, after being outlawed from Iceland, and for about four and a half centuries his descendants farmed sheep and cattle in the sheltered fjords of the south, building churches, a cathedral at Gardar, and large halls. The area is now part of the Kujataa landscape, inscribed as a World Heritage site in 2017, which shows how Norse farmers and the Inuit hunters who followed them each adapted to this fringe of the Arctic. Today sheep farms still dot the land, which makes Kujataa the only place in Greenland with real agriculture. The grass is green in summer, with wild flowers, and icebergs from the ice cap drift down the fjords.

Getting here has nothing in common with riding. Greenland has no road network between its towns, and Qaqortoq, the largest town in the south, with about three thousand people, is thirteen kilometres away by sea. Most visitors take a boat from Qaqortoq or hike a trail from Igaliku, and a few local tracks in and between settlements are the only places where a motorbike would be of any use. Plan for ferries, small boats and long walks. Weather is changeable, with fog, wind and cold rain, and a good waterproof jacket is far more useful than a riding one.

The visiting season is June to September, when the days are long, the mosquitoes are bearable and the boats run. At the ruin, take care not to climb on the walls, and leave nothing behind. Narsaq, a smaller town, has a supermarket and a bakery, and the lamb is excellent.

Kujataa is south Greenland at its gentlest, which is a relative term. The fjords here are deep, the mountains are steep, and the glacier is never far away, but in summer the valleys are green with grass and dotted with sheep. This is where Norse settlers from Iceland arrived in the tenth century, led, according to the sagas, by Erik the Red, and where Inuit hunters and Norse farmers lived within reach of each other for centuries. UNESCO listed the area in 2017 as a cultural landscape of farming at the edge of the habitable world.

The coordinates lie near Qassiarsuk, the place the sagas call Brattahlid, Erik's farm. There is a reconstructed turf church and a longhouse, and the foundations of the original settlement. Not far away is Igaliku, the old Gardar, once the seat of a Norse bishop, with the remains of a great hall and a cathedral. Hvalsey church, a medieval stone building with gables still standing, is one of the best-preserved Norse ruins in Greenland. The Norse colonies disappeared in the fifteenth century for reasons that are still debated, with climate, trade and conflict all suspected.

Riding is where I have to be straight with you. Greenland has no road network linking its towns. There are short gravel roads and tracks near villages, and from Narsarsuaq you reach Qassiarsuk by boat. A motorbike is not a practical way to explore this area, and the maps are best read as walking and boating routes. Narsaq, about thirty-seven kilometres away across the water, has fuel, a shop and a few places to eat, and Narsarsuaq has a former American airbase with the area's airport.

Summer is short and bright, with long evenings and mosquitoes, and the sheep farms are busy making hay. Icebergs drift in the fjords, and the weather can change in an hour. Take warm layers even in July. Arriving here feels like a very quiet kind of adventure, with turf walls, fjord water and a long view of ice.

Qassiarsuk is a sheep farming settlement of a few dozen people on the green side of a fjord in southern Greenland, and for a few years around the year 1000 it was the centre of European Greenland. The Norse chieftain Erik the Red, banished from Iceland for killing, arrived here in the 980s, built a farm that he named Brattahlíð, and became the leader of a colony that would eventually number several thousand. His son Leif, called the Lucky, sailed from here to the shores of North America.

You can see the story laid out on the grass. A modest replica of the small church that Erik's wife Thjodhild is said to have asked for stands beside the ruins of the farm, built of turf with a tiny window, and a long reconstructed Norse longhouse shows what living quarters looked like. A bronze statue of Leif stands on the hill. Greenland's Norse settlements vanished in the fifteenth century, and nobody knows exactly why, though colder climate and the decline of trade with Europe are thought to have played a part.

What strikes visitors even more is the setting. The Tunulliarfik fjord is wide, glittering and filled with icebergs that have floated down from the great ice sheet, and the hills are covered in dwarf birch and willow, and in July the farmland glows green. Summer days are very long, and the light is clear and cold. Midges can be fierce on still days, so a head net is worth the weight.

The ride question needs a straight answer. There are no roads linking Greenland's towns, and Qassiarsuk has no road out, so this point is reached by a short boat crossing from Narsarsuaq, where the airport grew from an American wartime base. Gravel tracks around the settlement are enough for walking and some cycling, and the practical way to visit is as part of a larger journey by plane and boat. Narsarsuaq has a small hotel, a museum and a few places to eat, but supplies are limited and prices high, so do not plan on improvising.

In the green fjords of South Greenland, roughly where the ice sheet meets sheep country, lie the ruins of a church that has outlasted the Norse people who built it. Hvalsey, known in Greenlandic as Qaqortukulooq, is the best preserved of all the Norse ruins in Greenland, its gable and walls of local stone still standing against the sky beside a quiet fjord. In 1408 a wedding was held here, and a letter written about it is the last written record of the Norse in Greenland. After that, silence, and no one is sure exactly what happened to the settlers.

I should be honest about the ride. There are no roads linking Greenland's towns, and no road to this site. Qaqortoq, the largest town in the south with about three thousand people, lies some thirty-eight kilometres away, and Narsaq is similar, but the way between them and Hvalsey is by boat across the fjord, or on foot or by quad along farm tracks. Motorcycles do not feature in this landscape in any normal sense. What you get instead is a boat trip and a short walk, with the meltwater streams, the smell of crowberry and grass, and the sound of gulls and sheep.

The setting is the real attraction. The land looks gentler than the popular picture of Greenland, with green pastures, birch and willow scrub, and the occasional drifting iceberg in the fjord. Summer, from June to August, brings long light, milder temperatures, and mosquitoes that can be a menace on still days. Weather changes quickly, with fog and wind arriving without notice, so boats may be delayed or cancelled. The farming tradition here is an old one: the Norse kept cattle, goats and sheep, and today's Greenlandic sheep farmers carry on the practice, which is part of the Kujataa cultural landscape that UNESCO recognised in 2017.

Practical matters rest in Qaqortoq, which has fuel, shops, a hotel and a harbour from which local boat operators run trips in the summer. Book in advance, since schedules are short, and carry warm clothing and waterproofs, plus insect repellent. Treat the ruins with care. They are protected, and the stones are delicate, so please do not climb on the walls. A quiet hour sitting beside the old church is the best way to feel the weight of a lost story.
